lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Noncommunicable Diseases, Causes and Risk Factors

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Describe what noncommunicable diseases are and determine their common causes.
- Identify symptoms, effects and prevention of noncommunicable diseases associated with malnutrition, poor working environment and exposure to drugs.

pages.title: What are Noncommunicable Diseases?
pages.body: A noncommunicable disease is a health condition that cannot be passed directly from one person to another, unlike an infectious disease caused by bacteria, viruses or other pathogens. Noncommunicable diseases typically develop gradually over time and are commonly linked to lifestyle factors, environmental exposure, or genetic predisposition, rather than being transmitted through contact with an infected person.

questions.q: A noncommunicable disease is best described as
o: A condition passed directly from person to person
A condition transmitted only through water
A health condition that cannot be passed directly between people
A type of infectious bacteria
questions.e: A noncommunicable disease is a health condition that cannot be passed directly from one person to another, unlike an infectious disease caused by bacteria, viruses or other pathogens.

pages.title: Common Causes of Noncommunicable Diseases
pages.body: Poor diet, lack of physical activity, tobacco and alcohol use, prolonged exposure to harmful substances at work, and genetic factors are common, broad causes underlying many noncommunicable diseases. Since these causes often build up their effects gradually, over months or years, noncommunicable diseases are frequently linked to long term habits and living or working conditions, rather than a single, identifiable moment of exposure.

pages.title: Diseases Associated with Malnutrition
pages.body: Malnutrition, meaning an unhealthy imbalance in diet, whether too little or too much of particular nutrients, can lead to noncommunicable diseases such as obesity, from excessive calorie intake relative to activity level, and conditions linked to nutrient deficiency, such as weakened bones from insufficient calcium or vitamin D. Symptoms and effects vary depending on the specific condition, but often include unusual weight change, fatigue, and weakened physical function over time. Prevention generally involves maintaining a balanced diet appropriate to one's activity level and nutritional needs.

questions.q: Malnutrition can contribute to noncommunicable diseases such as
o: Common cold only
Malaria only
Obesity or nutrient deficiency conditions
Tuberculosis only
questions.e: Diseases Associated with Malnutrition Malnutrition, meaning an unhealthy imbalance in diet, whether too little or too much of particular nutrients, can lead to noncommunicable diseases such as obesity, from excessive calorie…

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Diseases Associated with Poor Working Environments

pages.title: Diseases Associated with Poor Working Environments
pages.body: Prolonged exposure to dust, fumes, excessive noise, or repetitive physical strain in a poor working environment can contribute to noncommunicable conditions such as chronic respiratory problems, hearing loss, and musculoskeletal disorders affecting joints and muscles. Symptoms often develop slowly, such as gradually worsening breathing difficulty or joint pain, and effects can become permanent if the harmful exposure continues unaddressed. Prevention generally involves using appropriate protective equipment, improving ventilation, and following safe practices for repetitive or physically demanding tasks.

pages.title: Diseases Associated with Exposure to Drugs
pages.body:
Prolonged or harmful use of certain drugs, including tobacco, alcohol, and some medications when misused, is strongly linked to noncommunicable diseases such as liver disease, certain heart conditions, and some cancers, discussed further in the next lesson. Symptoms and effects again develop gradually with continued exposure, and prevention generally involves avoiding harmful drug use, following medical guidance when medication is genuinely needed, and seeking support to reduce or stop harmful habits where they have already developed.

[[pic:A three column comparison chart with columns headed Malnutrition, Poor Working Environment, and Drug Exposure, each column listing a small icon and brief label for a linked noncommunicable disease, a typical symptom, and a prevention strategy, allowing side by side comparison of the three risk categories discussed in this lesson.]]

Notice that although these three risk categories, malnutrition, poor working environments, and drug exposure, lead to quite different specific diseases, they share a common pattern, a build up of harmful exposure over time, gradually developing symptoms, and prevention strategies centred on reducing or avoiding the underlying risk factor.

pages.title: Analysing Risk Factors
pages.body: A risk factor is any characteristic, exposure, or behaviour that increases the likelihood a person will develop a particular disease, without guaranteeing that they definitely will. Analysing risk factors involves identifying which specific behaviours or conditions in a person's life increase their chances of developing a noncommunicable disease, and recognising that having several risk factors together, for example poor diet combined with a physically demanding, poorly protected job, can compound the overall risk more than any single factor alone.

pages.title: Named Noncommunicable Diseases, Their Signs and Prevention
pages.body:
| **GROUP** | **DISEASE** | **CAUSE** | **SIGNS AND EFFECTS** | **PREVENTION** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Malnutrition** | Kwashiorkor | Too little protein in the diet of a young child | Swollen belly and feet, thin limbs, thin reddish hair, poor growth | Give foods rich in protein such as beans, fish, eggs and milk |
| **Malnutrition** | Marasmus | Too little food of all kinds | Extreme thinness, wrinkled skin, weakness | Enough balanced food and breastfeeding of babies |
| **Malnutrition** | Obesity | More energy food than the body uses, with little exercise | Excess body fat. It raises the risk of diabetes, high blood pressure and heart disease | Balanced diet with less sugar and fat, and regular exercise |
| **Malnutrition** | Anaemia, rickets and goitre | Too little iron, too little vitamin D or calcium, and too little iodine | Tiredness and pale skin, soft bent bones, and a swelling of the neck | Leafy vegetables and liver, milk and sunlight, and iodised salt |
| **Lifestyle and diet** | Diabetes | The body cannot control the level of sugar in the blood. The common type is linked to excess weight and lack of exercise | Great thirst, passing urine often, tiredness, wounds that heal slowly. It can damage the eyes, kidneys and nerves | Healthy weight, exercise, less sugar, and regular checks |
| **Lifestyle and diet** | Hypertension, or high blood pressure | Too much salt, excess weight, stress, alcohol, smoking and lack of exercise | Often no signs. It can lead to stroke, heart failure and kidney disease | Less salt, exercise, no smoking, and regular checks of blood pressure |
| **Poor working environment** | Lung disease from dust, such as silicosis | Breathing in dust for years in mines, quarries, sawmills and cement works | Cough, shortness of breath, chest pain | Dust masks, wetting of dust, good ventilation |
| **Poor working environment** | Hearing loss, back pain and skin disease | Loud noise, heavy lifting and contact with chemicals | Deafness, pain and rashes | Ear protection, safe lifting, gloves and protective clothing |
| **Exposure to drugs** | Liver cirrhosis | Heavy drinking of alcohol over many years | Swollen belly, jaundice, liver failure | Avoid alcohol |
| **Exposure to drugs** | Lung cancer, heart disease and chronic bronchitis | Smoking tobacco, or breathing the smoke of others | Long lasting cough, breathlessness, chest pain | Do not smoke |
| **Exposure to drugs** | Addiction and mental illness | Abuse of drugs such as marijuana, tramadol and cocaine | Loss of control, poor school work, confusion, violence | Refuse drugs, choose good friends and seek counselling |

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Public health organisations, including the World Health Organisation, actively track noncommunicable diseases globally, since they now account for a very large proportion of deaths worldwide, often exceeding infectious diseases in many countries, making awareness and prevention efforts, of the kind studied in this lesson, an important part of both individual and public health strategy.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Cancer, Causes, Symptoms, Effects and Prevention

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Explain the causes, symptoms, effects and prevention of cancer.
- Identify common cancers that affect humans and link them to lifestyle.

pages.title: What is Cancer?
pages.body: Cancer is a noncommunicable disease in which certain cells in the body begin to grow and divide uncontrollably, forming abnormal masses of tissue called tumours, which can invade and damage surrounding healthy tissue and, in more advanced cases, spread to other parts of the body. Cancer can affect almost any organ or tissue, and the specific symptoms, effects and outlook vary considerably depending on where in the body it develops.

questions.q: Cancer is best described as
o: A condition where certain cells grow and divide uncontrollably
A type of common cold
A viral infection that spreads directly between people
An allergic reaction only
questions.e: Cancer is a noncommunicable disease in which certain cells in the body begin to grow and divide uncontrollably, forming abnormal masses of tissue called tumours, which can invade and damage surrounding healthy tissue and, in more…

pages.title: Causes of Cancer
pages.body: Exposure to tobacco smoke, excessive alcohol consumption, prolonged exposure to strong sunlight without protection, certain viral infections, exposure to harmful chemicals or radiation, and genetic factors inherited from parents are among the most commonly identified causes and risk factors for cancer. Many cancers develop from a combination of several of these factors acting together over an extended period, rather than from a single cause alone.

pages.title: Symptoms of Cancer
pages.body: Unexplained weight loss, persistent fatigue, unusual lumps or swelling, changes in the skin, such as a mole that changes shape or colour, persistent coughing or hoarseness, and changes in bowel or bladder habits are among the general warning symptoms sometimes associated with cancer, though these symptoms can also result from many other, less serious conditions, which is why proper medical diagnosis is essential rather than self diagnosis based on symptoms alone.

o: Assessed only by self diagnosis with no medical involvement

questions.e: Symptoms of Cancer Unexplained weight loss, persistent fatigue, unusual lumps or swelling, changes in the skin, such as a mole that changes shape or colour, persistent coughing or hoarseness, and changes in bowel or bladder…

pages.title: Effects of Cancer
pages.body: Damage to the organ or tissue where cancer develops, spread to other parts of the body if not treated early, significant physical and emotional strain on the affected person and their family, and, in advanced or untreated cases, death are serious potential effects of cancer, underscoring why early detection and treatment are so strongly emphasised in cancer awareness and prevention efforts.

pages.title: Prevention of Cancer
pages.body:
Avoiding tobacco use, limiting alcohol consumption, protecting skin from excessive, unprotected sun exposure, maintaining a healthy diet and regular physical activity, avoiding known cancer causing chemicals where possible, and attending recommended medical screenings for early detection are widely recommended strategies for reducing overall cancer risk, even though no single strategy can guarantee complete prevention in every case.

[[pic:A labelled poster style diagram with a central human body outline, small labelled markers pointing to common cancer sites (skin, lungs, breast, cervix, liver), and a surrounding ring of icons representing prevention strategies (no smoking, sun protection, healthy diet, regular screening), visually connecting cancer sites to relevant prevention actions.]]

Notice how prevention strategies are not identical for every type of cancer, for example sun protection is particularly relevant to skin cancer, while avoiding tobacco is particularly relevant to lung cancer, even though several strategies, such as a healthy diet, offer broader protection across multiple cancer types.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: Common Cancers and Their Link to Lifestyle

pages.title: Common Cancers and Their Link to Lifestyle
pages.body: Lung cancer, strongly linked to tobacco smoking, skin cancer, linked to prolonged unprotected sun exposure, liver cancer, linked to excessive alcohol consumption and certain viral infections, and cervical cancer, linked in part to certain viral infections, are examples of common cancers with a clear, well documented connection to specific, often modifiable lifestyle factors or exposures. Recognising these connections helps explain why public health campaigns so often focus on specific behaviour changes, such as reducing tobacco use or protecting skin from the sun, as practical, achievable ways to reduce cancer risk at a population level.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Early detection through regular medical checkups and screening significantly improves treatment outcomes for many types of cancer, since cancers caught at an early stage, before they have spread extensively, are generally far more treatable than those discovered only once symptoms have become severe, reinforcing why encouraging regular health checkups is such an important, ongoing public health message.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: The Concept of Health and Disease, and Common Diseases

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Define health as stipulated by the World Health Organisation, and show the relationship between health and disease.
- Conduct a survey about common diseases and analyse the findings to show what constitutes a common disease in a community.
- Identify causes, symptoms and prevention of common diseases.

pages.title: Defining Health
pages.body: The World Health Organisation defines health as a state of complete physical, mental and social wellbeing, and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity. This definition is important because it recognises that a person can be considered unhealthy even without a diagnosed disease, for example if they are experiencing significant mental distress or are unable to participate fully in their social and community life.

pages.title: Defining Disease
pages.body: Disease is any condition that disrupts normal body or mind function, typically producing specific signs and symptoms, and often having an identifiable cause, whether that cause is an infectious pathogen, an inherited genetic factor, or a lifestyle or environmental factor, as studied in the previous two lessons on noncommunicable disease and cancer.

pages.title: The Relationship Between Health and Disease
pages.body:
Health and disease exist along a broad, connected spectrum rather than as two entirely separate, unrelated categories, since the presence, absence, or severity of disease directly affects a person's overall physical, mental and social wellbeing, which is exactly what the World Health Organisation's definition of health is describing. A person can experience varying degrees of health even while managing a chronic disease, if their physical, mental and social wellbeing are otherwise reasonably well supported, which is why modern health care increasingly focuses on supporting overall wellbeing, not simply treating a single diagnosed disease in isolation.

[[pic:A simple diagram showing a horizontal spectrum, with Poor Health and Significant Disease labelled at one end, and Good Health and Wellbeing labelled at the other end, with a sliding marker positioned somewhere along the middle, and three small icons above the spectrum labelled Physical, Mental and Social, representing the three dimensions of health in the WHO definition.]]

Notice that health is presented as a spectrum, not a simple yes or no state, and that it depends on physical, mental and social wellbeing together, not on the absence of disease alone.

lessons.subject: sci
lessons.title: What Makes a Disease 'Common' in a Community?

pages.title: What Makes a Disease 'Common' in a Community?
pages.body: A common disease in a community is one that occurs frequently among the population of that specific community, often linked to local environmental conditions, prevailing lifestyle patterns, or limited access to prevention and treatment resources in that area. What counts as a common disease can vary considerably between different communities, since local factors such as climate, sanitation infrastructure, and economic conditions strongly influence which diseases occur most frequently in a given area.

pages.title: Conducting a Survey on Common Diseases
pages.body: Conducting a simple survey within a community, asking a representative group of people about illnesses they or their family members have experienced over a defined recent period, and then organising and analysing the results, can reveal which diseases are genuinely most common locally, rather than relying on assumptions or national level statistics that may not reflect specific local conditions. A well designed survey should ask clear, specific questions, protect the privacy of respondents, and be analysed carefully to identify genuine patterns rather than one off or unrelated individual cases.

questions.e: A well designed survey should ask clear, specific questions, protect the privacy of respondents, and be analysed carefully to identify genuine patterns rather than one off or unrelated individual cases.

lessons.title: Identifying Causes, Symptoms and Prevention of Common Diseases

pages.title: Identifying Causes, Symptoms and Prevention of Common Diseases
pages.body: Once a common disease in a community has been identified through a survey or other reliable evidence, systematically researching its typical causes, its recognisable symptoms, and established, effective prevention strategies allows individuals and community leaders to respond with informed, targeted action, rather than guesswork, addressing the specific disease burden actually affecting that community.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Ghana Health Service and similar public health bodies regularly collect and publish disease surveillance data at both national and regional levels, providing a valuable, more authoritative resource that a community survey, like the one conducted in this lesson, can be compared against, helping confirm whether local findings reflect broader regional or national health patterns.

pages.title: What you will learn
pages.body:
🎯 **By the end of this lesson you will be able to:**
- Discuss the nature of fungal diseases.
- Search for information on ringworm, candidiasis and fungal eye infection, including their mode of transmission from person to person, community to community, and from country to country.
- Describe the symptoms, effects and prevention of ringworm, candidiasis and fungal eye infection diseases.
- Describe the role of individuals, community members and government in managing these fungal diseases.
- Design and produce a poster to educate community members on the incidence and control of named fungal diseases.

pages.title: What Are Fungal Diseases?
pages.body: A fungal disease is an infection caused by fungi, microorganisms distinct from bacteria and viruses, that can grow on or within the human body, particularly favouring warm, moist environments such as skin folds, nails and mucous membranes. Fungal diseases are generally not life threatening in a healthy person, but they can be persistent, uncomfortable, and, in the case of eye infections, potentially serious if left untreated.

pages.title: Ringworm
pages.body: Ringworm is a fungal skin infection that produces a distinctive circular or ring shaped, red, itchy rash, most commonly appearing on the scalp, body, feet or groin, despite its name having no connection to actual worms. Ringworm spreads through direct skin contact with an infected person or animal, or through indirect contact with contaminated surfaces, clothing, or shared items such as towels and combs. Symptoms include itching, redness, and a slowly expanding, ring shaped rash, while prevention focuses on maintaining good personal hygiene, avoiding sharing personal items, and promptly treating infected pets, which can also carry and transmit ringworm.

pages.title: Candidiasis
pages.body: Candidiasis is a fungal infection caused by an overgrowth of a yeast normally present in small amounts on the skin and within the body, which can multiply excessively under certain conditions, such as a weakened immune system, prolonged antibiotic use, or a warm, moist environment. Candidiasis commonly affects the mouth, described as oral thrush, presenting as white patches on the tongue and inner cheeks, or the skin folds and genital area, presenting as redness, itching and discomfort. Prevention includes maintaining good hygiene, keeping skin folds dry, and using antibiotics only when genuinely necessary and as prescribed, since unnecessary antibiotic use can disturb the natural balance of microorganisms that normally keeps this yeast in check.

questions.e: Ringworm Ringworm is a fungal skin infection that produces a distinctive circular or ring shaped, red, itchy rash, most commonly appearing on the scalp, body, feet or groin, despite its name having no connection to actual worms.

pages.title: Fingernail and Toe Nail Infection
pages.body: Fungal nail infection occurs when fungi infect the nail bed, typically entering through small cracks in the nail or surrounding skin, and thrive particularly in the warm, often damp environment inside closed shoes. Symptoms include thickened, discoloured (often yellowish), brittle nails, sometimes with a distorted shape, developing gradually over an extended period. Prevention includes keeping feet clean and dry, wearing well ventilated footwear, avoiding walking barefoot in shared damp areas such as public showers, and treating any nearby fungal skin infection, such as athlete's foot, promptly to avoid it spreading to the nails.

pages.title: Fungal Eye Infection
pages.body:
Fungal eye infection, though less common than the fungal conditions already discussed, can occur when fungi enter the eye, often following an eye injury, particularly one involving plant material, or through contaminated contact lenses or lens solution. Symptoms include eye pain, redness, blurred vision, and unusual discharge, and this particular fungal disease is considered more serious than the others discussed in this lesson, since untreated fungal eye infections can threaten vision. Prevention includes practising careful contact lens hygiene, seeking prompt medical attention for any eye injury, particularly one involving plant matter or soil, and avoiding the use of contaminated or expired eye care products.

[[pic:A four panel labelled diagram, each panel illustrating one fungal disease discussed in this lesson, a ring shaped rash for ringworm, white patches on a tongue for candidiasis, a thickened, discoloured nail for nail infection, and a red, irritated eye for fungal eye infection, with a brief prevention tip listed beneath each panel.]]

Notice that while all four conditions are caused by fungi and favour warm, often moist conditions, they affect very different parts of the body and require somewhat different prevention approaches suited to the specific body part involved.

pages.title: Modes of Transmission, Person to Person, Community to Community, and Country to Country
pages.body: Fungal diseases such as ringworm typically spread from person to person through direct skin contact or shared personal items, and can spread from community to community as infected individuals travel, attend shared schools, or use shared public facilities such as showers or swimming pools. On a larger scale, international travel and the movement of people between countries can carry fungal infections across borders, which is one reason global health monitoring pays attention to the spread of persistent skin and nail infections, alongside more urgently dangerous infectious diseases.

pages.title: The Role of Individuals, Community Members and Government in Management
pages.body: Individuals can manage fungal disease risk through personal hygiene, prompt treatment of symptoms, and avoiding sharing personal items. Community members can support broader control by promoting hygiene awareness, ensuring shared facilities such as school showers are kept clean and dry, and supporting affected community members in seeking treatment rather than stigmatising visible skin conditions. Government plays a role through public health education campaigns, ensuring access to affordable antifungal treatment, and maintaining hygiene standards in public facilities such as schools, markets and healthcare settings.

pages.title: The Fungi Responsible and Further Facts
pages.body:
| **DISEASE** | **FUNGUS RESPONSIBLE** | **FURTHER FACTS** | **TREATMENT AND CONTROL** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ringworm** | Fungi that live on skin, hair and nails, known as Tinea | It is not caused by a worm. It forms itchy, ring shaped patches with a raised edge. It affects the scalp, the body, the groin and the feet, where it is called athlete's foot. It spreads by touch and by shared combs, towels, clothes and beds, and from pets | Antifungal cream or tablets. Keep the skin clean and dry and do not share personal items |
| **Candidiasis** | A yeast called Candida albicans | The yeast lives harmlessly on the body and overgrows when the defences of the body are weak, after long use of antibiotics, or in warm moist places. It causes white patches in the mouth, known as thrush, and itching with a whitish discharge in the genital area | Antifungal medicine. Good personal hygiene, loose cotton underwear, and antibiotics only when prescribed |
| **Fungal eye infection** | Moulds such as Fusarium and Aspergillus | It usually follows an injury to the eye by a plant, a stick or soil, or the use of dirty contact lenses or harmful eye drops. It causes pain, redness, discharge, blurred vision and sensitivity to light, and can lead to blindness | Urgent treatment at an eye clinic with antifungal eye drops. Protect the eyes on the farm and never put herbs or unprescribed drops in the eye |

Fungi grow best in warm, moist, dark places, which is why fungal infections are common between the toes, in skin folds and under tight clothing. Fungal diseases are not cured by antibiotics, which act only on bacteria.

pages.title: Going further
pages.body:
> 💡 **Going further**

Although fungal diseases such as ringworm and nail infections are rarely dangerous, they are extremely common worldwide and can significantly affect a person's comfort, confidence and quality of life if left untreated, which is why straightforward, low cost prevention habits, such as those studied in this lesson, remain genuinely valuable public health messages even though these conditions rarely make dramatic news headlines.
